Bulrushes
bool´rŭsh-ĕz
n. pl. (papyrus reeds of the Nile, woven into baskets and boats — Hebrew gome)
From bull (in the old sense of large or coarse) and rush. The Hebrew gome is the papyrus, the reed of Egypt from which baskets, boats and writing material were made.

Biblical Definition

Bulrushes are the papyrus reeds of the Nile, and the Authorized Version uses the word at the hinge of Israel's deliverance. Pharaoh had commanded that every Hebrew son be cast into the river. Jochebed obeyed the letter of the decree and defeated it: “when she could not longer hide him, she took for him an ark of bulrushes, and daubed it with slime and with pitch, and put the child therein; and she laid it in the flags by the river's brink” (Exo 2:3). The word for the little vessel is ark — the same word used of Noah's, and used nowhere else in Scripture. Both arks were daubed with pitch, both carried a deliverer through waters of judgment, and both were built by a believer acting on a word from God. Pharaoh's daughter came down to wash: “when she saw the ark among the flags, she sent her maid to fetch it” (Exo 2:5), and “when she had opened it, she saw the child: and, behold, the babe wept. And she had compassion on him, and said, This is one of the Hebrews' children” (Exo 2:6). Isaiah uses the same reed of Ethiopian diplomacy: a nation “that sendeth ambassadors by the sea, even in vessels of bulrushes upon the waters” (Isa 18:2). Empires travel in papyrus boats; so did the man who broke one.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a bulrush as a large kind of rush, growing in wet land or water, of which the ancients made baskets and small vessels; the papyrus of the Nile.

expand to see more

BULRUSH, n. A large kind of rush, growing in wet land or water, and without knots.

2. The papyrus of Egypt, of which the ancients made baskets, boats and paper.

ARK, n. A small close vessel, chest or coffer; also the vessel in which Noah and his family were preserved, and that in which Moses was set among the flags.

SLIME, n. Soft moist earth having an adhesive quality; bitumen, as used for mortar and for daubing.

Key Scripture

Exodus 2:3 — "And when she could not longer hide him, she took for him an ark of bulrushes, and daubed it with slime and with pitch, and put the child therein; and she laid it in the flags by the river's brink."

Exodus 2:5 — "And the daughter of Pharaoh came down to wash herself at the river; and her maidens walked along by the river's side; and when she saw the ark among the flags, she sent her maid to fetch it."

Exodus 2:6 — "And when she had opened it, she saw the child: and, behold, the babe wept. And she had compassion on him, and said, This is one of the Hebrews' children."

Isaiah 18:2 — "That sendeth ambassadors by the sea, even in vessels of bulrushes upon the waters, saying, Go, ye swift messengers, to a nation scattered and peeled, to a people terrible from their beginning hitherto; a nation meted out and trodden down, whose land the rivers have spoiled!"

Modern Corruption

The account is treated as a folk tale of an exposed infant, and the faith Hebrews credits to Moses' parents is emptied into maternal instinct.

expand to see more

Critical scholarship has long assimilated Exodus 2 to the ancient pattern of the exposed royal infant, and treated the ark of bulrushes as a legendary motif borrowed and retold. Hebrews 11:23 reads it otherwise and says why: by faith Moses, when he was born, was hid three months of his parents, because they saw he was a proper child; and they were not afraid of the king's commandment. That is a historical claim about the motives of two named people, and it makes the basket an act of faith and civil disobedience rather than a literary convention. Scripture's own commentary on its own narrative is the authoritative one.

The second thing the passage will not surrender is the sovereignty running through it. Pharaoh commanded the river; the river carried the deliverer to Pharaoh's own daughter, who paid the child's mother to nurse him and raised him in the palace of the man who meant to kill him. Every step of the rescue used the machinery of the persecution. This is not fate and not coincidence; it is the God who works all things after the counsel of His own will, and the ark of bulrushes is the small vessel in which He carried a nation's deliverance past a tyrant's decree.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew gome (H1573), papyrus, the bulrush of the Nile — Exodus 2:3, Isaiah 18:2, Isaiah 35:7, Job 8:11; tebah (H8392), the ark, used only of Noah's vessel and this one.

expand to see more

Hebrew gome (H1573) — papyrus, bulrush; Exodus 2:3, Job 8:11, Isaiah 18:2 and 35:7.

Hebrew tebah (H8392) — ark, chest; used in Scripture only of Noah's ark and the ark of bulrushes.

Hebrew chemar (H2564) and zepheth (H2203) — slime and pitch; the same daubing that sealed Noah's ark.

Hebrew suph (H5488) — flags, reeds; the same word as in the Red Sea, yam suph.

The choice of tebah rather than the ordinary word for basket is deliberate: two arks, two deliverances through water.

Usage

"“An ark of bulrushes… daubed with slime and with pitch” — the second ark in Scripture."

"“She laid it in the flags by the river's brink” — obedience to the decree that defeated it."

"“Vessels of bulrushes upon the waters” — empires travelled in the same reed."
